stem: A client develops wheezing, lip swelling, and a rapid weak pulse within minutes of eating a cookie containing nuts. Which hypersensitivity reaction is most consistent with this presentation?
rationale: The rapid onset after a likely allergen, plus wheezing, lip swelling, and weak pulse, points to an immediate IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction and possible anaphylaxis. Type IV reactions are delayed and T-cell mediated, type II reactions target antigens on cell surfaces, and type III reactions involve immune-complex deposition rather than this immediate airway/circulatory picture.
source: Immune/inflammation study guide; hypersensitivity PowerPoint text; saved immunity and practice exam quizzes

stem: Which white blood cells are classified as lymphocytes? Select all that apply.
rationale: B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells are the major lymphocyte groups emphasized in the immune materials. Neutrophils and basophils are granulocytes, so they are important white blood cells but not part of the lymphocyte category.
source: Immune/inflammation study guide; saved immunity quiz

stem: A client has difficulty swallowing a large capsule, so the nurse checks whether the medication is available as a liquid. Which medication right is the nurse primarily applying?
rationale: The problem is not the ordered amount or timing; it is whether the client can safely receive the medication in the prescribed form. Checking for a liquid formulation applies the right route/right formulation principle because swallowing difficulty can make a large capsule unsafe or impractical.
source: Foundations in Pharmacology study guide; medication safety PowerPoint text; saved mixed quiz

stem: A client with heart failure has dyspnea, cough, tachycardia, and crackles in the lung bases. Which side of heart failure do these findings most strongly suggest?
rationale: Left-sided failure backs blood into the pulmonary circulation, so lung findings such as dyspnea, cough, crackles, and low oxygen symptoms are expected. Right-sided failure is more associated with systemic venous congestion, such as peripheral edema, neck vein distention, hepatic engorgement, and nocturia.
source: Cardiology study guide; cardiovascular pathophysiology PowerPoint text; saved cardiovascular quizzes

stem: A client starts lisinopril for hypertension. Which teaching point is most important for the nurse to include?
options: Report swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or trouble breathing immediately.
Take an extra dose if blood pressure remains elevated after 1 hour.
Use potassium-containing salt substitutes freely to lower sodium intake.
Stop the medication once blood pressure readings are normal.
correctAnswers: Report swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or trouble breathing immediately.
rationale: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, and angioedema is a rare but high-priority adverse effect because swelling of the tongue, lips, face, or throat can obstruct the airway. Potassium-containing salt substitutes are unsafe without provider guidance because ACE inhibitors can raise potassium, and the client should not self-adjust or stop the medication just because blood pressure improves.
source: Cardiology study guide; cardiac meds PowerPoint text; saved cardiovascular pharmacology quiz

stem: A cardiac monitor shows a heart rate of 130/min with a sawtooth waveform. Which rhythm should the nurse suspect?
rationale: A sawtooth waveform is the classic rhythm clue for atrial flutter, often with a rapid ventricular response. Atrial fibrillation is usually irregularly irregular without organized sawtooth flutter waves, while PVCs and ventricular tachycardia are ventricular rhythms and would not match this atrial pattern.
source: Cardiology study guide; antiarrhythmic PowerPoint text; saved cardiovascular quizzes

stem: Which statement best describes ventilation?
options: Movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract
Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar membrane
Blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries
Oxygen use by cells to produce energy
correctAnswers: Movement of air into and out of the respiratory tract
rationale: Ventilation refers to air movement into and out of the respiratory tract. Diffusion is the movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar-capillary membrane, and perfusion is blood flow through the pulmonary capillaries, so those terms describe different parts of gas exchange.
source: Pulmonary study guide; respiratory pathophysiology PowerPoint text; saved respiratory quiz

stem: A client with asthma is having acute wheezing and shortness of breath. Which medication should the nurse expect to use first for rapid relief?
rationale: Acute wheezing and shortness of breath require a rescue bronchodilator, and albuterol is the short-acting beta-2 agonist used for rapid relief. Fluticasone reduces inflammation over time, salmeterol is long acting and not for rescue, and montelukast is a maintenance leukotriene receptor antagonist rather than immediate treatment for bronchospasm.
source: Pulmonary study guide; respiratory treatment PowerPoint text; saved mixed and respiratory quizzes

stem: Which adverse effects should the nurse include when teaching about first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine? Select all that apply.
rationale: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine cross into the CNS more readily and have anticholinergic effects, so dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, and sedation are key teaching points. Diarrhea and increased alertness do not fit the expected adverse-effect profile and would not be the best answers.
source: Pulmonary study guide; antihistamine PowerPoint text; saved mixed quiz

stem: A client has a large pulmonary embolism. Which ventilation-perfusion pattern is most likely?
options: High V/Q ratio due to dead space
Low V/Q ratio due to shunt
correctAnswers: High V/Q ratio due to dead space
rationale: With a pulmonary embolism, alveoli may still be ventilated but blood flow to that area is blocked, creating dead space. That produces a high V/Q ratio because ventilation is high relative to perfusion, whereas low V/Q or shunt physiology occurs when perfusion continues but ventilation is reduced.
source: Pulmonary study guide; ARDS/VQ PowerPoint text; saved practice exam

stem: A client with acute anxiety has ABG results: pH 7.55, PaCO2 27 mm Hg, and HCO3 24 mEq/L. Which acid-base imbalance should the nurse identify?
rationale: The pH of 7.55 is alkalotic, and the PaCO2 of 27 is low, so the primary problem is respiratory loss of carbon dioxide. The bicarbonate is normal, which means there is not a metabolic cause or meaningful renal compensation, making respiratory alkalosis the best interpretation.
source: Renal study guide; acid-base PowerPoint text; saved renal and mixed quizzes

stem: Which findings are recognized risk factors for chronic kidney disease? Select all that apply.
rationale: Hypertension and diabetes mellitus are major chronic kidney disease risks because high pressure and elevated blood glucose damage renal blood vessels and nephrons over time. Regular exercise, low sodium intake, and adequate hydration are generally protective or supportive strategies, not risk factors in this question.
source: Renal study guide; renal PowerPoint text; saved renal quiz

stem: A client is prescribed furosemide for fluid overload. Which teaching should the nurse prioritize?
options: Take the medication early in the day.
Increase potassium salt substitutes without checking with the provider.
Expect urine output to decrease after the dose.
Stop the medication when edema improves.
correctAnswers: Take the medication early in the day.
rationale: Furosemide is a loop diuretic, so it increases urine output and can disrupt sleep or increase fall risk if taken late in the day. The client should not self-stop it when edema improves, and potassium changes require monitoring rather than unsupervised salt substitutes or supplements.
source: Renal study guide; fluid and diuretics PowerPoint text; saved mixed renal case

stem: Which factors are recognized causes or major contributors to peptic ulcer disease? Select all that apply.
rationale: Peptic ulcer disease is strongly associated with H. pylori infection, NSAID-related loss of gastric mucosal protection, and excess acid states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Hypertension and constipation may be clinically relevant problems, but they are not primary mechanisms for ulcer formation.
source: GI study guide; upper GI PowerPoint text; saved GI quiz

stem: Which factors increase a client's risk for constipation? Select all that apply.
rationale: Constipation risk increases when stool movement or stool bulk is reduced: opioids slow motility, low fiber decreases bulk, immobility reduces bowel activity, and obstruction can physically impair passage. High fluid intake usually supports softer stool and is more preventive than causative.
source: GI study guide; GI PowerPoint text; saved GI quiz

stem: A client with acute kidney injury has decreased erythropoietin production. Which CBC finding should the nurse expect?
options: Decreased white blood cell count only
rationale: Erythropoietin from the kidney stimulates bone marrow production of red blood cells. If acute kidney injury decreases erythropoietin, red cell production can fall, leading to lower hemoglobin and hematocrit; platelet or isolated white blood cell changes would not be the direct expected CBC pattern.
source: Coagulation/hematology study guide; anemia PowerPoint text; saved hematology quiz

stem: The nurse is monitoring a client at risk for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which labs are most important to follow?
options: Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time
correctAnswers: Platelet count, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time
rationale: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors, so platelet count, PT, and PTT help track the abnormal clotting and bleeding process. Electrolytes, glucose, albumin, or hemoglobin A1c may matter for other conditions, but they do not best monitor the coagulation changes central to DIC.
source: Coagulation/hematology study guide; anemia/coagulopathy PowerPoint text; saved hematology quiz

stem: Which pathophysiologic change is central to type 1 diabetes mellitus?
options: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing insulin deficiency
Excess cortisol production causing insulin resistance
Overproduction of thyroid hormone increasing metabolism
Increased aldosterone secretion causing sodium retention
correctAnswers: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causing insulin deficiency
rationale: Type 1 diabetes is driven by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, which causes an absolute insulin deficiency and leads to hyperglycemia and risk for ketoacidosis. Cortisol excess, thyroid hormone excess, and aldosterone excess point toward other endocrine disorders rather than the central mechanism of type 1 diabetes.
source: Endocrinology study guide; endocrine PowerPoint text

stem: A client with hypothyroidism is prescribed levothyroxine. Which outcome best indicates the medication is replacing the deficient hormone?
options: Improved energy and normalization of thyroid hormone levels
Immediate relief of acute chest pain
Rapid bronchodilation during an asthma attack
correctAnswers: Improved energy and normalization of thyroid hormone levels
rationale: Levothyroxine is thyroid hormone replacement, so the expected therapeutic effect is gradual improvement in hypothyroid symptoms such as low energy and normalization of thyroid hormone markers. It does not provide immediate chest pain relief, acute bronchodilation, or rapid diuresis; those effects belong to other medication classes.
source: Endocrinology study guide; endocrine PowerPoint text

stem: A client is prescribed an antibiotic and reports a history of a severe penicillin allergy. What is the nurse's priority action before administering the first dose?
options: Verify the allergy reaction and clarify whether the ordered antibiotic is safe to give.
Administer the dose because all antibiotic classes are unrelated to penicillin.
Hold all medications until the infection resolves.
Teach the client that allergies only matter with injectable antibiotics.
correctAnswers: Verify the allergy reaction and clarify whether the ordered antibiotic is safe to give.
rationale: A severe penicillin allergy must be clarified before giving an antibiotic because some related agents may be unsafe depending on the reaction and drug ordered. Allergies matter for oral and injectable routes, and the nurse should not simply give the dose or stop all therapy; the priority is verification and clarification before administration.
source: Infection PowerPoint text; GI PowerPoint note on penicillin allergies; medication safety materials
